n5-aka.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the ground cracking open on the mountain trail, and underneath it the Earth is glowing — lit from below by a fire you can't see. That heat pushes up through the soil until the whole hillside burns a deep, angry <radical>red</radical>. Earth glowing under a fire: red.
n5-aka.reading_mnemonic: The guy who lit that underground fire is Seki, and he's coughing his lungs out from the smoke — a wet, rattling <reading>せき</reading> that won't stop as long as the red embers keep burning. Every time he sees red he starts up again: せき, せき, せき.
n5-aka.description: Means "red"; a common color kanji that shows up in words for the color itself and things like traffic lights.

n5-ame-rain.meaning_mnemonic: Look through the window frame and watch the drops falling inside it, one after another down the glass. Those little drops caught in the frame are all you need to picture. Drops falling inside a window frame: <radical>rain</radical>.
n5-ame-rain.reading_mnemonic: A cow gets caught outside in the downpour and lets out a long, miserable "<reading>う</reading>ー" as the drops soak her. Every time it rains, that cow's soggy うー is the sound you hear.
n5-ame-rain.description: Means "rain"; the base kanji for weather words and it sits on top of many other weather-related characters as a component.

n5-ao.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a tiny sprout pushing up over the <radical>moon</radical>. It's young, fresh, and glowing that impossible color between <radical>blue</radical> and green — the shade of new leaves at dusk. That youthful sprout-over-moon is blue-green.
n5-ao.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, holds up a jar of blue-green ink and says the color is called 「<reading>せい</reading>」 — of course she knew it first. She's already dipping her perfect brush in before anyone else can answer.
n5-ao.description: Means blue or green (the fresh blue-green range); shows up in color words and in compounds about youth and freshness.

n5-ashi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>mouth</radical> perched on top of a pair of <radical>stopping</radical> legs — the legs have skidded to a halt, and the mouth is barking orders down at them. Those legs end in one thing: a <radical>foot</radical>. That mouth-over-stopping-legs shape is your foot, your leg, the thing you plant when you've had just enough.
n5-ashi.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named Sok is nursing a blister on her foot. Every painful step she counts out loud, 「<reading>そく</reading>、そく、そく」, until she finally reaches the vending machine at the top and decides that's enough walking for one day.
n5-ashi.description: Means foot, leg, or to suffice/be enough; shows up in words for body parts and in verbs about having sufficient amounts.

n5-atarashii.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>spicy</radical> man hauls his pepper skewer into the showroom, eyes streaming, swearing the sauce is mild. Behind him a <radical>tree</radical> sits on the plinth, dug up roots and all, sap still wet where the <radical>axe</radical> took the branch off this morning — the blade is still buried in the chopping block by the door. The attendant <radical>standing</radical> beside it throws both arms out so nobody touches anything. Just cut, just felled, just unwrapped: everything in here is new.
n5-atarashii.reading_mnemonic: The showroom greeter is Shin, and every time a new model rolls in he shouts his own name — <reading>しん</reading>! — as he yanks the cover off. Whatever Shin unveils is always brand new.
n5-atarashii.description: Means "new"; a very common kanji appearing in words for new things, newspapers, and freshness.

n5-bun-minute.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter prises the chipped <radical>sword</radical> out of its frozen rice cake, wipes it down, and hands it one shot at redemption: a log. It comes down clean, and the two halves lean away from each other in a fresh <radical>eight</radical>. One minute, one log, two parts, and the sword finally understands what it is for.
n5-bun-minute.reading_mnemonic: The woodcutter, sawdust in her eyebrows, times herself at one log a minute and calls it the most <reading>fun</reading> you can have before breakfast. The sword, back in her hands and still chipped, snorts <reading>ふん</reading> — it was the one doing all the work.

n5-chikara.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this single stroke and picture a bent arm flexing hard — the elbow cocked, the muscle bulging. That one flexed arm is all you need to see: it's pure <radical>power</radical>.
n5-chikara.reading_mnemonic: A weightlifter named Rio steps up to the bar and gives a warrior's yell as she flexes: "<reading>りょく</reading>!" The whole gym feels the raw strength in that shout.
n5-chikara.description: 力 and 九 are both two strokes with a hook, and the hooks point opposite ways. 力 starts with a flat horizontal that turns down and hooks to the left, with a slash cutting through it. 九 starts with a short slash, then a stroke that curves right and flicks upward.

n5-dai-big.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing with their arms flung out and their legs spread as wide as they can go, straining to show you just how huge the fish they caught was. That whole stretched-out stick figure is this character. When someone stands like that, they're always telling you one thing: it was big.
n5-dai-big.reading_mnemonic: The person is stretching so wide because they're measuring Dai, the giant baby, who is the size of a truck. You gasp <reading>だい</reading> as he cries an earthquake and you realize nothing has ever been this big.
n5-dai-big.description: All four share the same spread-armed figure. 大 is the bare shape. 太 adds a dot underneath, 犬 adds a dot at the top right, and 天 caps it with an extra horizontal above the arms. If nothing has been added, it is 大.

n5-denki-den.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>rain</radical> is hammering your window, four dashes frozen mid-fall on the glass, and out beyond it the farmer's flooded <radical>rice field</radical> lies there like a giant square battery, the dirt paths chopping it into four bright plots. A bolt splits the sky, hits the water, and every plot lights up at once — the whole grid crackling with electricity.
n5-denki-den.reading_mnemonic: The lightning hits a power line and the whole street goes DEN — <reading>でん</reading> — every fluorescent tube in Koichi's konbini surging bright at once. You feel that でん in your teeth as the electricity floods back.
n5-denki-den.description: Means "electricity"; shows up in everyday words for trains, phones, lights, and anything electrical.

n5-deru.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you see one <radical>mountain</radical> stacked right on top of another mountain — two sets of three peaks piled up. When the peaks get that tall, there's only one thing you want to do: get out and leave. So this doubled-up mountain means exit, leave.
n5-deru.reading_mnemonic: At the exit of the mountain trail stands a hiker who sneezes so hard every time someone leaves — a huge "<reading>しゅつ</reading>!" — that the whole vending machine rattles. Every time you head for the exit, you hear that "しゅつ" behind you.
n5-deru.description: Means exit or leave; shows up in everyday words about going out, leaving, and departures.

n5-do-earth.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a simple cross being pushed straight down into the ground, staking out a plot of dirt. The moment its base sinks in, the loose brown stuff piles up around it. That cross pressed into the ground is <radical>earth</radical>, plain soil.
n5-do-earth.reading_mnemonic: A gardener drops to his knees in the plot and starts digging with his bare hands, going "do, do, do" (<reading>ど</reading>) as he flings soil over his shoulder. Every heavy handful he tosses out lands with that same low ど grunt.

n5-dokusho.meaning_mnemonic: On the left the <radical>speech</radical> is doing its usual thing, sentence after sentence stacking out of that little mouth. On the right the armoured <radical>samurai</radical> duck has climbed down off the garden wall onto a pair of sturdy <radical>human legs</radical>, a blanket <radical>cover</radical> pulled snug over his shoulders against the draught. He isn't listening to a word of it — his eyes run down the stacked lines, top to bottom, silently. That is not hearing speech. That is reading it.
n5-dokusho.reading_mnemonic: The reader you find hunched over those lines of speech is a poison-pen critic, and you nickname her Doku (<reading>どく</reading>) because every review she reads she then tears apart. Watch her read a page and you can practically see the どく venom drip off her pen.

n5-eki-station.meaning_mnemonic: You're waiting on a platform when a galloping <radical>horse</radical>, mane flowing and all four legs pounding, thunders straight past you and onto the tracks. It has to hurdle the <radical>body</radical> sprawled across the end of the bench, the same commuter who faceplanted hours ago and has refused to get up since. The conductor sighs — every day here, horses on the rails and sleepers on the benches. Where else but the station?
n5-eki-station.reading_mnemonic: A commuter named Eki misses the last train and shouts "<reading>えき</reading>! えき!" across the empty platform, hoping the station master will hear her and hold the doors.
n5-eki-station.description: Means "station" — the word for a train or subway station, seen constantly in place names and on transit signs.

n5-en.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character straight on: it's a rounded <radical>box</radical>, a coin flattened into a frame. Picture a single shiny coin held tight inside a square window, so perfectly round it's almost a circle. That coin is a yen, and its round shape is the circle.
n5-en.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the beeping till spits out change, and a friend named En scoops up every round coin, grinning "these <reading>えん</reading> are mine." Every time you hear the till beep, picture En pocketing えん.
n5-en.description: Means yen (Japan's currency) and also circle or round; shows up on money, prices, and words for round shapes.

n5-furui.meaning_mnemonic: Above the <radical>mouth</radical> balances a little <radical>cross</radical> of stacked crossbars, like the beams of a house that's been standing for centuries. Every mouth that has passed through here has told the same worn-out story, over and over. A mouth held up by ancient timber can only mean one thing: old.
n5-furui.reading_mnemonic: Koichi finds an ancient rice ball at the very back of his konbini shelf, so far past its date the wrapper has yellowed. He picks it up, sighs, and mutters just one syllable at how old it is: 「<reading>こ</reading>」.
n5-furui.description: Means "old," as in old and worn from age; appears in words about age and antiquity and in the common word for "used/secondhand."

n5-gaku.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a swaddled <radical>child</radical>, arms out, parked under a low <radical>cover</radical> of scribbled notes and diagrams, tucked in at the edges the way that blanket drapes over a sleeping cat. Nothing gets out from under it but the sound of pencil scratching. A child kept all day beneath a canopy of lessons is study and learning.
n5-gaku.reading_mnemonic: At the school, the star pupil Gaku is the one who never stops studying, and everyone in the echoing hallways calls out <reading>がく</reading> whenever they need the answer. Hear がく and you hear the kid who lives to learn.
n5-gaku.description: Means study or learning; a very common kanji that shows up in words for student, school, and academic subjects.

n5-gatsu.meaning_mnemonic: Look up on a clear night and there it is: a thin crescent hanging in the dark, the <radical>moon</radical>. Watch that crescent fatten, fade, and swing back around, and you've just watched one whole month go by. This character is that crescent — so it means moon, and it means month.
n5-gatsu.reading_mnemonic: A gecko has claimed the moon as its own, scuttling across the crescent every night. Whenever it does, you hear its little feet go <reading>げつ</reading>, げつ against the pale surface. That gecko-on-the-moon sound is how you remember げつ.
n5-gatsu.description: Means moon or month; a common kanji that shows up in dates, days of the week (Monday), and countless month-related words.

n5-go-language.meaning_mnemonic: On the left, <radical>words/speech</radical> is already pouring out — a <radical>mouth</radical> releasing stacked lines of speech. On the right, another open mouth joins in, adding its own noise. When mouths keep stacking speech on top of speech like this, what you get is a whole language, packed with word after word.
n5-go-language.reading_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till at Koichi's konbini, a chatty regular named Go won't stop talking — every single language pours out of him at once, and the only word you catch is his own name, <reading>ご</reading>, ご, ご.

n5-go.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and picture a hook or a hand reaching sideways to snag things off a shelf. Now imagine you're grabbing snacks that way — one, two, three, four, and with that last crooked pull you land your fifth. That little hooked shape is you catching five things in one swipe.
n5-go.reading_mnemonic: The kid counting up his catch is Go, and once he hits five he throws his hands up and yells "<reading>ご</reading>!" like it's the winning number. Every time he lands a fifth thing, out comes that triumphant ご.
n5-go.description: The kanji for five, the number 5, seen everywhere from prices and dates to counting and phone numbers.

n5-hachi.meaning_mnemonic: Look at those two strokes leaning away from each other, spreading apart at the bottom like legs mid-stride. They're <radical>splitting</radical>, opening wider and wider — and the wider they split, the bigger the number gets. That spread lands you on eight.
n5-hachi.reading_mnemonic: A honeybee — a <reading>はち</reading> in Japanese — drifts down to the onigiri shelf in Koichi's konbini and lands on exactly eight of them, one after another. You count the buzzing little はち as it goes: eight stops, eight onigiri.
n5-hachi.description: The same two falling strokes, arranged three ways. 八 leaves a clear gap at the top with both strokes leaning apart. 人 joins them into one peak. 入 tucks the short stroke under the long one so the top overhangs.

n5-hairu.meaning_mnemonic: Watch the shape closely: it's a little figure ducking their head as they pass under a low doorway. You lean, you dip, you step through — and just like that, you <radical>enter</radical>.
n5-hairu.reading_mnemonic: The figure ducking through the door is a new student, and as they enter the echoing school hallway everyone whispers "the new one, <reading>にゅう</reading>, the new one." Every time someone new enters, that にゅう ripples down the hall.
n5-hairu.description: 入, 人 and 八 are the same pair of strokes. In 入 the short left stroke begins partway down the long one, leaving a small overhang at the top. 人 meets at a clean point, and 八 never lets the two touch.

n5-hana.meaning_mnemonic: A fresh patch of <radical>grass</radical> is sprouting out of the soil the way it always does, two clumps poking up over one line of dirt — except this morning one clump has gone rogue and shot a tall stem straight up with a wide open bloom on the end, petals spilling over sideways. The rest of the grass sits underneath it looking embarrassed. Grass with a blossom bursting out of the top of it is a flower.
n5-hana.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands right in the middle of the flowerbed and lets out a proud 「<reading>か</reading>」, singeing every petal within reach. Now the only flower left standing is the scorched one under her claws.
n5-hana.description: Means "flower"; a very common everyday kanji seen in words for flowers, plants, and blossoms.

n5-hanashi-wa.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> releasing stacked lines of <radical>speech</radical> leans in close, and right beside it a <radical>tongue</radical> sticks out of a mouth, wagging nonstop. Put the speech next to the busy tongue and you've got someone who just won't stop talking, spinning story after story.
n5-hanashi-wa.reading_mnemonic: Wanda the storyteller loves an audience, so she waves both hands and calls out "<reading>わ</reading>!" every time she starts a new tale. That little "わ" is her signal that another long talk is about to begin.
n5-hanashi-wa.description: Means talk or story; shows up in everyday words for speaking, conversation, and telephone.

n5-hantime.meaning_mnemonic: Two matchsticks lie crossed on the counter making that little <radical>ten</radical> mark, and a cleaver comes down straight through the middle of it. What's left is a fat upright with two legs kicked out symmetrically at the top, one left and one right, each side mirroring the other exactly. Ten cut clean down the centre, sliced into two equal parts, is half.
n5-hantime.reading_mnemonic: Han, the half-and-half chef, holds up a plate where one side is rice and the other is curry, split exactly down the center. "<reading>はん</reading>!" he barks, tapping the dividing line — because to Han, half is the only portion worth serving.
n5-hantime.description: 半 and 羊 both sit horizontal bars on a vertical under a split top. Count the bars: 半 has two, 羊 has three. That extra horizontal is the only reliable difference.

n5-hayai.meaning_mnemonic: Someone has scratched the <radical>ten</radical> mark into the dirt — two matchsticks crossed, the tally you cut when you've counted both hands — and stood it upright like a fencepost. Behind it the <radical>sun</radical>, that window with a bar in it, comes climbing up to start a new <radical>day</radical> and clears the top of the post before you've counted anywhere near ten. It's up hours ahead of your alarm, and now everything you do today has to be fast: early, fast.
n5-hayai.reading_mnemonic: There's a rooster at Grandma Kane's shrine who crows the moment the sun peeks over the mossy steps, way too early: "<reading>そう</reading>! そう!" he screams, so loud the cats scatter. Now you're up before dawn whether you like it or not.
n5-hayai.description: Means "early" or "fast," and shows up in everyday words about time and speed like 早い (early/fast) and 早く (quickly).

n5-hidari.meaning_mnemonic: A badger in a hard hat stands on the level <radical>ground</radical> of the <radical>construction</radical> site while the crane lowers the steel I-beam toward its slot. His right hand is busy holding a sandwich, so he steadies the swinging girder with the other one, arm braced flat and taking the whole weight. That steadying hand is the hand on the left.
n5-hidari.reading_mnemonic: A samurai marches into Koichi's konbini and slams down a coin with his left hand, barking "<reading>さ</reading>!" as he demands the last onigiri. Every time you see this kanji, hear that samurai's sharp さ ringing off the beeping till.
n5-hidari.description: Means "left," the opposite of right; shows up constantly in directions and in the compound 左右 (left and right).

n5-hidariuma.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the sundial standing on the <radical>ground</radical> — that single flat line is the earth beneath it. A pole rises up from that ground, and right at the top of the day its shadow points straight down at the line, casting no shadow at all. When the shadow vanishes onto the ground like that, you know it's exactly noon.
n5-hidariuma.reading_mnemonic: At high noon a golfer named Gordon lines up his shot and yells "<reading>ご</reading>!" as he swings, because he can't wait until the sun drops. His voice echoes across the empty midday field: ご, ご, ご.
n5-hidariuma.description: All three are bars on a vertical under a slanting flick. 午 has two bars and its vertical stops at the upper one. 牛 also has two, but its vertical pushes up above the top bar. 千 has only one bar.

n5-higashi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>sun</radical> rising and getting tangled in the branches of a <radical>tree</radical> on the horizon. You see the sun caught right behind that tree first thing in the morning — and the sun always comes up in the east. Sun plus tree, hung together at dawn: that's east.
n5-higashi.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker faces the sunrise and lets out a long, tired yawn — a huge "<reading>とう</reading>" that echoes down the slope. Every morning she climbs to greet the east with that same sleepy とう.

n5-hito-jin.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape: two legs, mid-stride, walking forward and carrying nothing else along with them. That's the whole picture — a body up top, two legs striding out beneath. Two legs walking forward is a <radical>person</radical>.
n5-hito-jin.reading_mnemonic: Jin, the friendly giant, is the biggest person you'll ever meet, ducking through every doorway just to say hello. When you spot this character, picture him waving down at you and hear the giant himself: <reading>じん</reading>.
n5-hito-jin.description: 人 is the two-stroke figure that meets at a single clean peak. 入 slides its short stroke down the long one so the top overhangs, and 八 keeps the two strokes apart with a gap between them.

n5-hoku.meaning_mnemonic: The tortoise is out on the balcony again with its hand mirror, squinting at the two cracks on its own shell and announcing by <radical>divination</radical> that tonight will be clear. So the hedgehog drags its fork out under the thin crescent moon for another <radical>evening</radical> of trying to take a bite out of it. Neither of them is going back in until the reading is finished, so both sit there in the cold with the fence at their backs — firmly outside.
n5-hoku.reading_mnemonic: You lock yourself out of Koichi's konbini after hours and a guy named Guy comes tapping the glass from the cold, calling "<reading>がい</reading>! I'm still stuck out here!" He is very much on the outside.
n5-hoku.description: Means "outside"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words for the outdoors and things that are external.

n5-hon.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>tree</radical> standing tall, and then draw the <radical>ground</radical> right across its trunk — a single flat line marking exactly where the roots meet the soil. That line points to the tree's source, the very origin it grew from. And the thing that captures a story's origin, pressed flat from a tree, is a book.
n5-hon.reading_mnemonic: A monk named <reading>ほん</reading> sits on the mossy steps at Grandma Kane's shrine, reading the same book over and over. Every time a cat brushes past, he mutters "ほん, ほん" without looking up — he cannot put that book down.
n5-hon.description: 本 is 木 with one extra stroke: a short horizontal laid across the lower trunk. Nothing else changes, so that little bar down at the base is the only thing to look for.

n5-hyaku.meaning_mnemonic: Put the <radical>number one</radical> on top of a ray of light so bright it turns <radical>white</radical>, and look what happens: that single one stacked over the white glow multiplies into a whole crowd. One little stroke sitting above all that whiteness isn't just one anymore — it's a hundred.
n5-hyaku.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a hiccuping cook keeps counting onigiri, and every time he hits a full tray he lets out a huge "<reading>ひゃく</reading>!" — a hiccup and a yell in one, because a hundred rice balls is a lot to hiccup through.
n5-hyaku.description: 百 is 白 with one extra stroke on top. 白 caps its box with a small flick; 百 turns that cap into a full-width horizontal bar.

n5-ichi.meaning_mnemonic: One flat line of hard-packed dirt stretches across an empty plain. Standing dead centre on that <radical>ground</radical>, as always, is the smug goat — the only creature in the world, as far as she is concerned. Today she is holding a talent show: one contestant, one stage, one judge, all of them her. She accepts the prize from herself, which is a mouthful of the dirt she is standing on. One stroke, one goat, one winner: one.
n5-ichi.reading_mnemonic: The talent show finally gets an audience: a sunburnt hiker called Itchy, who has exactly one mosquito bite, right between his shoulder blades where his hands cannot reach. He sits down on the flat line of ground, scratches his back against the goat, and groans <reading>いち</reading>, いち, いち in time with every scrape.
n5-ichi.description: Beyond the plain counting number, 一 carries a wider sense of a single thing taken as a whole, so it turns up in words about being first, being the same, or doing something all at once. Write it as one confident horizontal stroke, left to right, and keep it flat and reasonably long — short or slanted, it starts to look like a fragment of some other character.

n5-iku-go.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a stick figure caught mid-stride, legs split wide, one arm swinging forward — the whole character leans into the <radical>step</radical>. That's a person who won't stand still, always moving to the next place. When you see this shape, you see someone about to go.
n5-iku-go.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, can't sit still either — the second a shelf goes empty he's out the door to go restock it, muttering "<reading>こう</reading>, こう, keep it moving." Wherever he needs to go, he goes at a run.
n5-iku-go.description: Means "go" and shows up constantly in verbs of movement and travel, such as 行く (to go).

n5-iu-gen.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the bottom of this character and you'll find a <radical>mouth</radical>, wide open. Above it, stacked up in neat horizontal lines, is everything that mouth is pushing out — layer after layer of <radical>speech</radical>. A mouth releasing stacked lines like that is exactly what it means to say a word.
n5-iu-gen.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a general in full armor climbs the mossy steps and won't stop giving orders — every word out of his mouth is a barked command. The cats scatter as the general says "<reading>げん</reading>!" like it's the only word he knows.

n5-jikan-ji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> climbs its window over the shrine to start another <radical>day</radical>, and its shadow falls across a signpost hammered into a patch of <radical>earth</radical>. Somebody has laid the carpenter's ruler flat in the soil beside it, thumb pinning it down, and ticks off one more <radical>inch</radical> every time the shadow creeps forward. Sun, post and ruler together turn plain dirt into a clock — which is how you measure time, hour by hour.
n5-jikan-ji.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful clockmaker named Jiro keeps every timepiece in Koichi's konbini ticking, and each hour on the hour he shouts "<reading>じ</reading>! じ!" as the alarms go off. Whenever you need to know the time, you listen for Jiro's じ.
n5-jikan-ji.description: Means time or hour, and shows up everywhere you talk about clock time and telling the hour.

n5-juu.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you see one perfect plus sign, one clean <radical>cross</radical>. That plus sign is the mark you use when you count all the way up to a full set on your fingers — two hands, all of them raised. A single cross standing tall like this means ten.
n5-juu.reading_mnemonic: A judo champion bursts into Koichi's konbini and slaps down exactly ten coins on the beeping till, shouting <reading>じゅう</reading> with each one. Every time you picture that plus-sign cross, hear the judo master's じゅう ringing out.
n5-juu.description: 十 is a plain cross: one flat horizontal and one straight vertical. 千 adds a slanting flick above the bar. 七 bends the second stroke instead, curving it right and flicking upward at the end rather than running straight down.

n5-ka-fire.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing with their arms flung out, and sparks are flying off them in every direction. They're crackling, glowing, throwing off heat — this is a person who has become <radical>fire</radical>. Every time you see 火, see that sparking figure and think: fire.
n5-ka-fire.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and lets out a puff of flame with a raspy caw: 「<reading>か</reading>!」. The flame and the sound arrive together, so when you see this fire kanji, you hear Kaa's か.

n5-kaeru.meaning_mnemonic: You push your own front door open and the <radical>broom</radical> is still going, three stiff prongs driving crumbs and one indignant cat down the hallway, exactly as you left it this morning. The cat gives up and burrows under its <radical>cover</radical> on the porch. On the hook your rectangle of <radical>cloth</radical> hangs in two long folds, limp, waiting. You take it down and wipe the day off your face. Coming back to the same broom, blanket and cloth is what it is to return.
n5-kaeru.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, has been out riding the wind all day, and now she giggles as she slips back inside her old tree with a soft <reading>き</reading>. Watch her return home and you'll hear that き every time.
n5-kaeru.description: Means "return," as in going or coming back home; the core kanji in the verb 帰る, to return.

n5-kaku-write.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>brush</radical> is back on your desk, three prongs clamped round its shaft, still flecked with ink from the certificate it ruined. You dip it, and the <radical>sun</radical> — that window with a bar in it — sinks below the edge of your notebook, its last light lying flat across the page. Line after line goes down under that glow until the whole <radical>day</radical> is on paper. Sun on the page, brush in your fist: that is write.
n5-kaku-write.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands on your notebook and squints at your terrible handwriting, muttering "<reading>しょ</reading>, しょ" every time you smudge a letter. Each little puff of flame dries the ink so you can keep writing.
n5-kaku-write.description: Means "write"; shows up in words about writing, documents, and books, like 書く (to write).

n5-kane-gold-dup.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole <radical>village</radical> at dusk — its stacked paddies, its slab of packed earth, its wooden houses — huddled over one big cooking fire. The smoke climbs and stains every wall until the sooty village standing over that fire has settled into one single color: <radical>black</radical>.
n5-kane-gold-dup.reading_mnemonic: The soot-covered villagers cough up thick black lungfuls, hacking <reading>こく</reading>, こく into the night air. Every cough is darker than the last — that's the sound of black.
n5-kane-gold-dup.description: Means "black"; the everyday word for the color (くろ) and a common on'yomi こく in compounds.

n5-kau.meaning_mnemonic: You spot something you want, so you reach for the cowrie <radical>shell</radical> that once worked as money. You lay that shell on the counter and slide it across. Handing over the shell-money is how you buy.
n5-kau.reading_mnemonic: The moment you buy your onigiri at Koichi's konbini, Kaa the fire-breathing crow swoops in and shrieks 「<reading>ばい</reading>」 as if saying "bye-bye" to your cash before you've even paid.
n5-kau.description: Means "buy," the verb 買う (to purchase); shows up constantly in shopping and everyday transactions.

n5-kawa.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and squint: three flowing lines running side by side down the page. That's water moving — three currents carving their way through the land. Three flowing lines: a <radical>river</radical>.
n5-kawa.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank you meet a fisherman who has cast a line into every one of those three currents. He grins and tells you he's caught a thousand — <reading>せん</reading> — fish today, one for each ripple in the river.
n5-kawa.description: Means "river"; a common N5 kanji seen in nature words and countless place names.

n5-ki-spirit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a little puff of <radical>steam</radical> curling up off a hot bowl of rice — that swirling, rising shape is exactly this character. You can almost see the wisp lifting into the air, alive and moving. That invisible thing rising off warm things is the very idea of spirit and energy.
n5-ki-spirit.reading_mnemonic: The steam curls up and out pops Kiki, the tree spirit, giggling as the wind stirs her branches. She rides that rising energy on a breeze of 「<reading>き</reading>」.
n5-ki-spirit.description: Means spirit or energy; a very common kanji found in words about mood, feeling, weather, and vitality.

n5-kiku-hear.meaning_mnemonic: You press your <radical>ear</radical> right up against a <radical>gate</radical> to catch the whispers on the other side. The wood is cold, but you hold still, straining that one ear against the swinging doors. When you press an ear to a gate like this, you're doing two things at once: you hear, and you're dying to ask what's going on.
n5-kiku-hear.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the scholarly rabbit twins, press their ears to the gate to hear you ask a question — and immediately start arguing about the answer. "<reading>ぶん</reading>!" they squeak in unison, because those two never agree on anything they overhear.
n5-kiku-hear.description: 聞 and 間 are the same gate frame with different things standing inside it. 聞 puts 耳, an ear, in the gateway. 間 frames the sun there instead. What the gate contains is the whole difference.

n5-kin.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a solid little roof, and buried right underneath it the <radical>king</radical>'s own skewered stack of crowns, gems still crusted on, with two loose nuggets shaken off into the dirt beside it. A roof over a buried king is exactly what this character shows you: precious <radical>metal</radical> tucked away where nobody digs. Turn it up and you've got gold and money.
n5-kin.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane keeps her real fortune under the shrine's giant bell, and every time a cat brushes it, it goes <reading>きん</reading>. That soft きん ring is the sound of gold sitting safe underneath.

n5-kita.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon has finally landed. It came down in a snowdrift at the top of the map, still gripping the bent <radical>spoon</radical> it levered out of the ice cream tub, and it's now sitting back-to-back with a second raccoon on a frozen bench, both hunched away from each other against the gale — which is exactly the shape of this character. The <radical>spoon</radical> is frozen solid to its paws. That wind is coming straight down from the north.
n5-kita.reading_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the wind off the northern peak is so brutal that a hiker named Hoku pulls his hood tight and mutters "<reading>ほく</reading>, ほく" through chattering teeth as he trudges. Hear him — ほく — every time you point north.

n5-ko-child.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's a swaddled baby with its little arms flung out to the sides. That bundled shape wriggling and reaching is exactly what this kanji is — a <radical>child</radical>.
n5-ko-child.reading_mnemonic: A child at the riverbank keeps splashing everyone, so you press a finger to your lips and go "<reading>し</reading>!" — the sound you make to shush a rowdy kid. That soft "し" is how you hush this child.
n5-ko-child.description: Means "child"; a very common kanji appearing in words for children and as a frequent name ending.

n5-kon-now.meaning_mnemonic: You spot a <radical>person</radical> walking forward under a wide roof that shelters them from the rain. They don't dwell on where they've been or where they're headed — under that roof, in this exact spot, all that matters is the present moment. A person taking cover means: now.
n5-kon-now.reading_mnemonic: Right now, this very second, Koichi is slamming down onigiri prices at the konbini and yelling "<reading>こん</reading>!" like a battle cry to get you buying before the moment passes. Every time you hear こん, you know it means now, now, now.
n5-kon-now.description: 今 and 会 wear the same wide roof. Under it 今 has only a short stroke and a small hook. 会 packs a fuller body beneath the roof, with a horizontal bar and legs below it.

n5-kou-school.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tree</radical> stands in the middle of the courtyard, roots gripping the soil, one wide branch spread over the whole yard. Your <radical>father</radical> has dragged the barbecue out under it, tongs held high in both hands, announcing lunch to four hundred children at once, and he's snapped the pot <radical>lid</radical> down over the grill by its little knob so the smoke doesn't set off the alarm in the hallway. Bells, classrooms, homework and dad grilling under the tree — this is school.
n5-kou-school.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, has set up a pop-up shop right inside the school gate, restocking onigiri between classes and muttering <reading>こう</reading>, こう as he lines up the shelves. The kids buy their lunch from him before the bell.

n5-kuchi.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character: it's just an open square, a hole with nothing inside. Picture it as a <radical>mouth</radical> hanging wide open, mid-yawn or mid-shout. An open square, an opening — a mouth.
n5-kuchi.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, leans across the beeping till and shouts an order to his stock boy, his mouth wide open: 「<reading>こう</reading>!」 Every time he barks like that, you picture that gaping mouth and hear こう.
n5-kuchi.description: Means "mouth" or "opening"; a common N5 kanji that shows up in words about mouths, entrances, and exits.

n5-kuni.meaning_mnemonic: Picture an <radical>enclosure</radical>, a closed box with walls around everything inside, and set the <radical>jewel</radical> — that skewered stack of crowns, gems and all — down in the middle of it. Draw those walls big enough and you're no longer fencing a garden; you're fencing a whole people in around their crown. Walls wrapped around a king give you a country.
n5-kuni.reading_mnemonic: At the border of this walled country stands a guard named Koku, who stamps every passport with a cheerful <reading>こく</reading> sound. No stamp, no entry — こく, こく, all day long.
n5-kuni.description: Means "country" or "nation"; a very common kanji seen in words for countries and citizenship, read こく in compounds and くに on its own.

n5-kuru-rai.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>tree</radical> standing at a crossroads with two little travelers resting under its branches, one on each side of the trunk. The tree can't move, so it waves the travelers over: "Come! Come to me, sit in my shade." Everyone always comes to the tree.
n5-kuru-rai.reading_mnemonic: The traveler who comes to the tree is Rye, and he never arrives quietly — he shouts "<reading>らい</reading>, I'm here!" as he strolls up the path. Whenever someone comes into view down the road, listen for that らい.
n5-kuru-rai.description: 来 is 米 with an extra horizontal across the top. Count the horizontal bars: 米 has one, 来 has two.

n5-kyuu.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and see a hook curling forward, the kind of cane you'd hang up after a long day. Picture yourself at the bottom of the mountain trail, counting the switchbacks left before the top: one, two, all the way up to that last brutal bend that looks exactly like this hooked shape. You lean on your cane at bend nine, and that curl is the number nine.
n5-kyuu.reading_mnemonic: At bend nine on the mountain trail you finally reach the vending machine, but your legs give out — you go "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" as you collapse against it. That sharp little cry of relief at spot nine is exactly the sound きゅう.
n5-kyuu.description: 九 and 力 are both two strokes with a hook, hooking opposite ways. 九 opens with a short slash, then a stroke that curves right and flicks upward. 力 opens with a flat horizontal that turns down and hooks to the left, with a slash cutting through it.

n5-ma-interval.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>gate</radical> with its two swinging doors thrown open. Right in the gap between them, the <radical>sun</radical> is hanging low, filling the opening with light. That sliver of sun caught in the gate is the space between things — an interval, the gap between.
n5-ma-interval.reading_mnemonic: A guard named Kan stands watch in that gateway, timing exactly how long the sun lingers in the gap. Every time the interval passes he shouts "<reading>かん</reading>!" and slams one door shut.
n5-ma-interval.description: 間 and 聞 are the same gate frame with different contents. 間 sets 日, the sun, inside the gateway. 聞 stands an ear there instead. What is framed by the gate settles it every time.

n5-machi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture this whole character as a bird's-eye view of a settlement: a neat grid of <radical>rice fields</radical> on the left pressed up against a straight main road running down the right. Fields plus a road is the smallest complete place people can live in — that's a town.
n5-machi.reading_mnemonic: The town mayor climbs onto a soapbox in the square and announces he's the big chief now: "I'm in charge — call me <reading>ちょう</reading>!" Every time you walk into this town, you hear that same booming ちょう echoing off the buildings.
n5-machi.description: Means "town" and shows up in place names and words for local districts and neighborhoods.

n5-mae.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a fancy storefront with a wide awning over the sidewalk, and set into the wall beneath it that tall narrow window with two bars across the middle. The crescent <radical>moon</radical> has drifted down and wedged itself inside the frame, glowing there like a display piece. It is in position before opening, before the staff, before anyone, hanging out ahead of the whole shop and greeting you before you step inside. That shape is front, and before.
n5-mae.reading_mnemonic: A calm Zen monk stands out front of the shop, arriving before everyone else, and he bows and murmurs <reading>ぜん</reading> as he settles into place. He's always in ぜん — front and center, before the doors open.
n5-mae.description: Means front or before; extremely common in words for physical position (in front of) and time (before, previous), such as before an event or the front of a building.

n5-mai-every.meaning_mnemonic: A wind-up alarm clock is bolted to the pole outside the station, and every morning that <radical>mother</radical> leans out of the departing train window, posts a forgotten lunchbox onto the pole, and shouts reheating instructions over the ringing. Same train, same pole, same hour, without fail. That relentless, clockwork repetition is exactly what this character means: every.
n5-mai-every.reading_mnemonic: The clock belongs to Mai, who winds it every morning and shouts "My time!" as it rings. Hear her name <reading>まい</reading> as the sound that hammers home the routine — every day, まい, まい, まい.
n5-mai-every.description: Means "every" and shows up in common time words for recurring events, such as every day, every week, and every morning.

n5-man.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single hook-shaped banner snapping in the wind above a market stall. On that one banner, someone has painted a running tally that just keeps climbing — past a thousand, past nine thousand, until the whole cloth is crammed with zeros. That one impossibly loaded banner stands for ten thousand.
n5-man.reading_mnemonic: A street vendor named Manny throws his arms wide under that banner and yells, "Man, I've sold ten thousand of these!" You can hear the <reading>まん</reading> right there in his ecstatic "Man!" as the crowd surges in.
n5-man.description: 万 and 方 share a horizontal over a hooked stroke. 万 is just those two: a flat bar, then a stroke that drops and hooks left. 方 adds a dot on top and a short slash, so it runs to four strokes against 万's three.

n5-me-eye.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's an upright frame with two pupils sitting inside it. Tip it on its side and it even looks like it's staring right back at you. That frame with pupils is exactly what it is — an <radical>eye</radical>.
n5-me-eye.reading_mnemonic: A woodcarver named <reading>もく</reading> is whittling a tiny wooden eye at Koichi's konbini counter, holding it up to inspect the grain. Every time he blinks, he mutters "もく, もく" as he lines the carving up with his own eye.
n5-me-eye.description: Count the bars inside the box. 目 is tall with two horizontals. 日 has one. 自 is 目 with a small slash added on top of the box.

n5-meiname.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the balcony the hedgehog is out with its fork again, watching the crescent get bitten away for the <radical>evening</radical>, and it still cannot remember what the thief is called. So it leans over the railing, opens its <radical>mouth</radical> as wide as it goes, and yells the one word that fills the gap. An evening sky plus a mouth shouting into it gives you a name.
n5-meiname.reading_mnemonic: A performer named Mei struts into Koichi's konbini and belts out "<reading>めい</reading>, that's my name, don't wear it out!" She spells it letter by letter until the whole shop knows exactly who she is.
n5-meiname.description: 名 and 多 both start with the same slanted three-stroke piece. 名 finishes with a small closed box beneath it. 多 repeats that slanted piece a second time instead, so it is one shape stacked twice.

n5-michi.meaning_mnemonic: The giraffe in the business suit is late, so it lowers its telescoping <radical>neck</radical> flat to the ground and lets the winding <radical>road</radical> unroll straight along the top of it, spots and all. Commuters simply walk up the giraffe and keep going, and by lunchtime nobody can tell where the animal ends and the way forward begins — this kanji is road, the way.
n5-michi.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the road you meet a doe standing in the middle of the path, blocking the way. She won't budge, so you call out "<reading>どう</reading> do I get past you?" — and the doe just chews and stares, owning the whole road.
n5-michi.description: Means road or way; a very common kanji seen in words for streets, paths, and figurative "ways" of doing things.

n5-migi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the flat horizon line of the <radical>ground</radical>, and a hand reaching down under it into an open <radical>mouth</radical> to pull something free — the fingers and the little box of the mouth locked together in one shape. That hand is always your dominant one, the one you shove in to grab a stuck snack. It's the hand on the right.
n5-migi.reading_mnemonic: You reach for the last onigiri on Koichi's shelf with your right hand and your fingers close on nothing but air, so you let out a soft "<reading>う</reading>う" of disappointment. That little "うう" is the sound you make when your right hand comes up empty.
n5-migi.description: 右, 左 and 石 all park something under a two-stroke top. 右 and 左 differ in what sits below: 右 has a small box, 左 a short cross-like piece. 石 shares 右's box but writes the top as a cliff, the horizontal running along the top with only its left end turning down.

n5-mimi.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you'll spot a dangling shape hanging off the side of a head. That soft, drooping flap catching every sound is an <radical>ear</radical>.
n5-mimi.reading_mnemonic: A jittery DJ named Jiji cups a hand to his ear and shouts "<reading>じ</reading>, じ, do you hear that beat?" — the sound goes straight into his ear as じ.
n5-mimi.description: Means "ear"; the body part, and shows up in words about hearing and listening.

n5-minami.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody has upended a <radical>wide box</radical> on the hot sand, and across its flat top two matchsticks are laid in a <radical>cross</radical>, like the world's worst weather vane. A flamingo nudges the box round and round all afternoon, and the arm of the cross that ends up warmest is the one pointing south.
n5-minami.reading_mnemonic: A backpacker named Nan has been hiking down the mountain trail for days, always heading south toward warmer weather. Every time someone asks which way she's going, she just points and sighs, "<reading>なん</reading>... south, always south." The word なん sticks because Nan won't stop saying it.

n5-miru.meaning_mnemonic: Take an <radical>eye</radical> (目) and stand it up on a pair of <radical>human legs</radical> (儿), and suddenly it can walk around anywhere it wants. Where does an eye on legs go? Out into the world, to look at everything. So this is what it means to <radical>see</radical>.
n5-miru.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, drags you over to his wall of antique swords because he wants you to see his newest one. "<reading>けん</reading>! けん!" he barks, pawing at the blade until you finally look.
n5-miru.description: Means "see" and is the base of the common verb 見る (to see/look); it shows up constantly in everyday words about looking and watching.

n5-moku.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character and you can see it whole: a single vertical trunk, roots digging down at the bottom and branches reaching out to the sides. Stand back and the shape is unmistakable — a <radical>tree</radical>.
n5-moku.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, giggles as she climbs to the very top and peeks over the leaves — she's playing "<reading>もく</reading>" (peekaboo), disappearing behind branches every time the wind blows. Whenever you spot this tree, hear her whisper もく from up in the canopy.
n5-moku.description: 木 is the bare tree: a horizontal, a vertical, and two strokes sweeping down from the crossing. 本 is exactly this plus one short horizontal laid across the lower trunk.

n5-nagai.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the whole character: it's an old man standing side-on, with a flowing beard and long hair streaming down past his shoulders, and a walking stick planted at the bottom. He's the eldest, the one everyone else follows — so this is your picture of something <radical>long</radical>, and of the elder who leads.
n5-nagai.reading_mnemonic: That long-bearded elder is the leader of a whole troupe of butterflies, and he lets one land on his flowing hair — a <reading>ちょう</reading> (butterfly). Every time you see this kanji, picture the ちょう resting on the leader's long locks.
n5-nagai.description: Means long or leader; shows up in words for length, seniority, and being the head of something, like a school principal or a company chief.

n5-naka.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>mouth</radical>, that open square, and now imagine a single spear driven straight down through its center. The line splits the opening into two even halves, landing dead in the middle. Whatever you skewer that cleanly is right in the middle, tucked inside.
n5-naka.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse, refuses to guard the door or the back — he plants himself squarely in the <reading>ちゅう</reading>, the very middle of the room, so no threat can slip past on either side. "The center is where a loyal mouse belongs," he squeaks.
n5-naka.description: Means middle or inside; extremely common, appearing in words about being in the middle of doing something, insides, and locations like the center of town.

n5-nana.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon is still airborne, still gripping that bent <radical>spoon</radical>, and the handle has come out of the ice cream twisted into a crooked hook. Someone hammers it into the wall by the door and hangs exactly seven coats on it. When it sags under all that weight, you know what it is holding: seven.
n5-nana.reading_mnemonic: A shy cat at Grandma Kane's shrine will only come out when you call it exactly seven times — and each time you call, you shush the other cats: <reading>しち</reading>, しち, quiet now. By the seventh しち, it finally pads down the mossy steps.
n5-nana.description: 七 and 十 are both a bar crossed by a second stroke. 十 keeps that stroke straight, running top to bottom. 七 bends it: it drops, curves right, and flicks upward at the end.

n5-nen.meaning_mnemonic: The scarecrow in the field is propped up on a warrior's shield, that flat board left out in the sun until it is cracked and completely <radical>dry</radical>. It has stood there watching the rice grow, get harvested, and grow again, straight through the full turn of the seasons. One complete loop of that dry board's silent watch is a year.
n5-nen.reading_mnemonic: A tired farmer counts the passing seasons by taking a nap in the shade of that scarecrow each time the harvest ends. He mumbles "<reading>ねん</reading>、ねん" — like the sleepy sound of nodding off — once for every year that rolls by.
n5-nen.description: Means "year"; a very common kanji appearing in dates, ages, and words about time.

n5-ni.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon is back at the same noodle shop table, its broth going cold. Look at 二 and you are looking at its handiwork: one short flat line laid neatly above one longer flat line, the snapped-off half of a chopstick above the whole one it was never separated from. A second raccoon slips in, sees the arrangement, and snaps its own chopstick so the table will match. Four paws, nobody eating: <radical>two</radical>.
n5-ni.reading_mnemonic: The waiter is Niko, a tired man who stopped being surprised by raccoons years ago and now simply keeps score. He carries out the second bowl, sets it beside the first, taps the table once and says <reading>に</reading>, flat as a bell — the way you announce a total rather than a discovery. The raccoons now snap chopsticks purely to hear him do it.
n5-ni.description: 二 is the plain counting two, used for quantities, dates, prices and floors. Its spoken form shifts with the counter that follows, so the same character sounds different in a date than in a count of objects. Write it as two level horizontals, top to bottom, the lower one clearly longer — that length difference is the whole character, and the two strokes never touch.

n5-nichi.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the character: it's a window with a bar across the middle. Through that window you can see the <radical>sun</radical> climbing into the sky, and once the sun is up, a whole new day begins. Window plus bar, sun in the frame — that's a day.
n5-nichi.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat wakes at dawn and greets the rising sun with the same cry every morning: "<reading>にち</reading>! にち!" The others answer, and that's how the whole shrine knows a new day has started.
n5-nichi.description: Check the top and count the bars. 日 is a plain box with one horizontal inside. 白 is the same box with a small flick added on top. 目 has no cap but carries two horizontals instead of one.

n5-nichiyou.meaning_mnemonic: You flip your calendar and the <radical>sun</radical> is sitting bright at the left edge, marking the day, while someone sweeps the rest of the square clean with that stiff-pronged <radical>broom</radical>, cat still asleep across the top prong. Every morning the sun climbs up, the broom shoves yesterday off the grid, and the fresh square gets its label. Each swept-and-sunned box is one named weekday.
n5-nichiyou.reading_mnemonic: Yoko, exhausted, groans "no more, no more" as she crosses off day after day on the wall calendar. Every square she reaches she moans <reading>よう</reading>, よう, because to her every single weekday feels the same.

n5-nishi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a squat bird cage with a little bird perched inside, its legs dangling below the frame. At sunset the birds all fly home to roost, settling in the cage as the sun sinks in the same direction. That cage where everything comes to rest for the night points you toward the west.
n5-nishi.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, insists she always knows exactly where the sun sets, so she marches to the western edge of the sports field at dusk and points, calling out 「<reading>せい</reading>, that way!」 while the whole class watches the sky turn orange behind her.
n5-nishi.description: 西 and 四 are both boxes with strokes inside. 四 is a plain rectangle with two short legs bending inward. 西 sits an extra horizontal bar across the very top, above the box, which 四 never has.

n5-nomu.meaning_mnemonic: On the left is the radical for food and eating, and on the right is a person opening their mouth wide in a <radical>yawn</radical>, a lack. But this yawning mouth isn't tired — it's tipping a glass back, mouth wide open to gulp something down. When you see food beside that gaping, thirsty mouth, you drink.
n5-nomu.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a regular named Inn slaps a cold can on the beeping till and says the same thing every single day: "First, I drink!" You can hear the 「<reading>いん</reading>」 right at the front of Inn's name as he cracks it open.
n5-nomu.description: Means "drink"; the everyday kanji in the verb 飲む, to drink.

n5-onna.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at the character and you'll see a figure kneeling gracefully, one arm sweeping across, the other resting low. That elegant kneeling pose is exactly how you were taught to spot a <radical>woman</radical>.
n5-onna.reading_mnemonic: A woman named Jo sweeps into Koichi's konbini and orders in a booming voice, "<reading>じょ</reading>, that's me!" The whole shelf of onigiri rattles as she says it, so じょ is stuck to this woman for good.
n5-onna.description: Means "woman"; a very common N5 kanji that appears in words for females and in compounds relating to girls and women.

n5-ooi-ta.meaning_mnemonic: The hedgehog is back on the balcony with its fork, watching the crescent get bitten away for the <radical>evening</radical>, when a second <radical>evening</radical> stacks up underneath the first, leaning like a lopsided snowman. One moon is never enough. It wants another, and another, until the plate is piled high. Two stacked and still craving more: that is how you get many.
n5-ooi-ta.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, Ta counts the coins in the improbable vending machine, and there are far too many to hold. "<reading>た</reading>, た, た," she taps each one as they spill from her hands — there are just too many.
n5-ooi-ta.description: 多 is the same slanted piece written twice, one stacked below the other. 名 writes that piece once and puts a small closed box underneath it instead.

n5-otoko.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>rice field</radical> stretching out under the sun, and the one person out there doing the heavy lifting. He bends his arm, flexes his <radical>power</radical>, and drags the plow across the paddies all day. Someone with that much power working the rice field — that's the man.
n5-otoko.reading_mnemonic: The man out in the field takes a break and starts pounding out a rhythm on his empty water bucket: <reading>だん</reading>, だん, だん. Every man on the trail can hear that drumbeat and grins.

n5-roku.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>number eight</radical> standing tall, and then set a little <radical>lid</radical> right on top of it. That lid caps the eight and knocks it down two — from eight, you drop to six. The lid on top of eight always means six.
n5-roku.reading_mnemonic: A rock star climbs onto the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and belts out six songs to the empty air. Every time he screams "<reading>ろく</reading>!" a cat appears, until six of them are yowling backup. That rock (ろく) show is how you hear six.
n5-roku.description: Means six; the basic number 6, seen everywhere from counting and prices to dates and times.

n5-san.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and count what you see: <radical>three</radical> flat lines stacked neatly on top of each other. One line, then another, then a third. Three lines means, simply, three.
n5-san.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful ranch hand named San lines up three fence rails on the mountain trail, tapping each one and calling out 「<reading>さん</reading>」 as she checks the count. Three rails, three, and San says the number every time.
n5-san.description: The kanji for three, the number 3, appearing constantly in counting, dates, and prices.

n5-sei-life.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single seed pushed into the <radical>earth</radical> — that cross of soil where everything begins. A green shoot cracks through and reaches up out of the ground. From that patch of earth, something new is born: this is life.
n5-sei-life.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, is the first sprout to shoot up every spring, hand raised before anyone else has even woken. When the teacher asks who's most full of life, Sei（<reading>せい</reading>）is already standing, beaming.
n5-sei-life.description: Means "life" or "birth"; a very common kanji that shows up in words about living, being born, students, and fresh or raw things.

n5-sen.meaning_mnemonic: Take the plus sign for <radical>ten</radical> and lay a single slash across its top, like one bold pen-stroke scratched over it. That one extra mark turns humble ten into something enormous — you've just multiplied it a hundredfold. Ten with a lid on top means a thousand.
n5-sen.reading_mnemonic: A senator named Sen shows up at the shrine and drops a thousand coins into the offering box all at once. "That's from all my constituents," she says, "<reading>せん</reading> of them exactly." Every time you see this kanji, hear Sen bragging about her せん coins.
n5-sen.description: Count the horizontals and look at the top. 千 has one bar under a slanting flick. 十 has one bar and no flick, just a straight cross. 午 and 干 both carry two bars — 午 under a flick, 干 starting flat.

n5-sensei-saki.meaning_mnemonic: You spot two <radical>legs</radical> left standing without a body, striding out the door ahead of everyone else. No torso to slow them down — those legs are always one step in front, gone before you've even moved. Whatever they're doing, they did it previous to you and they're already ahead.
n5-sensei-saki.reading_mnemonic: Those bodiless legs sprint down the mountain trail so far ahead they trip a wire and set off a whole line of fireworks — <reading>せん</reading>, せん, せん — bursting one after another to mark how far in front they already are.

n5-sha-car.meaning_mnemonic: Look straight down at a cart from above: one long axle running through the middle, wheels flanking each side, a boxy frame around it all. That's exactly what this character is — a cart seen from overhead with its axle drawn right through it. Trace that shape and you're looking at a <radical>vehicle</radical>.
n5-sha-car.reading_mnemonic: A show-off racer revs his engine outside Koichi's konbini and shouts "Watch me!" — but he peels out so fast all you hear is a screech of "<reading>しゃ</reading>!" as the vehicle vanishes down the street. Every time you see this car kanji, that "しゃ!" is the last sound it makes.
n5-sha-car.description: 車 and 重 are the same boxy stack, but 重 is taller and runs an extra horizontal through the middle. Count the horizontal strokes crossing the body: 重 always has one more than 車.

n5-shi-city.meaning_mnemonic: You stroll into the town square and above every stall hangs a bright piece of <radical>cloth</radical> on a rod, snapping in the wind. On the biggest stall a pot steams away, and the vendor keeps slamming the flat disc of its <radical>lid</radical> back down over the rim so nobody smells the stew for free. Rows of cloth and clanging lids stretch as far as you can see. This is the heart of the city, its bustling market.
n5-shi-city.reading_mnemonic: The busiest stall belongs to Shi, a sharp-eyed vendor who greets every shopper crossing the market with a cheerful 「<reading>し</reading>!」. Follow her voice and you'll always find the center of the city.
n5-shi-city.description: Means city or market; shows up in words for towns and municipal places like 市 (city) and city names.

n5-shiro-white.meaning_mnemonic: You step outside Koichi's konbini and the morning sun hits you full in the face — a ray of light so bright everything goes pure <radical>white</radical> for a second. You blink, and the whole world is still washed out and white. That blinding ray is your picture for white.
n5-shiro-white.reading_mnemonic: The dazzling light spooks a startled hawk perched on the konbini roof; it beats its wings once and goes, <reading>はく</reading>, hacking out a cough as it flaps into the too-bright sky. Hear that はく every time you see this pure white flash.
n5-shiro-white.description: All four are the same box with bars inside, and the top settles it. 白 caps the box with a small flick. 百 turns that cap into a full-width horizontal. 自 uses a short slash instead. 日 has no cap at all.

n5-shita.meaning_mnemonic: The tortoise props its hand mirror flat on the level <radical>ground</radical>, squints at the two cracks running along underneath it, and announces the week's forecast by <radical>divination</radical>. The prediction never changes: everything worth knowing is under that line, in the space beneath your feet. That little crack hanging below the horizon points exactly where to look, which is down, below.
n5-shita.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, dives straight down off the power line and lets out a sharp 「<reading>か</reading>」 as she plummets toward the ground below. Every time she drops down, that same caw of 「か」 rings out.
n5-shita.description: Means down or below; a very common kanji appearing in words about lower position, direction, and going down.

n5-shou-small.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single hook standing upright with two dots flanking it, one on each side, like something delicate pinched between two fingertips. It's so slight it could vanish if you sneezed. That tiny hook with its two little dots is the very picture of <radical>small</radical>.
n5-shou-small.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, snaps his white glove and shrinks the whole set until the doves look like specks. As everything gets impossibly small, the crowd gasps, "<reading>しょう</reading>!" — the man himself is the smallest thing on stage.
n5-shou-small.description: 小 is three strokes: a hooked vertical with a short dash on each side. 少 is 小 with a fourth stroke, a slash sweeping down to the left beneath it. If there is a tail, it is 少.

n5-shu-week.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a boxy calendar page laid flat, and the winding <radical>road</radical> comes sweeping in and threads across it, square to square, through all seven days. You put your own footsteps down on it and <radical>advance</radical> one box at a time until the road curves right back to where it started. One full loop of that road around the little grid is exactly one week.
n5-shu-week.reading_mnemonic: A woman named Shu (<reading>しゅう</reading>) plans her whole week on that looping calendar path, and every seven days she sighs "しゅう, another one done!" as she starts the loop again. Hear her say しゅう each time the week resets.

n5-sui.meaning_mnemonic: Stand at the riverbank and watch the streams splashing outward in every direction, cold spray hitting your face. Those wild, branching streaks are the whole picture: <radical>water</radical>.
n5-sui.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a swimmer named Sui dives in and shouts "<reading>すい</reading>!" as the cold hits, then keeps splashing everyone within reach. Every time you see this kanji, hear Sui hollering すい from the water.

n5-sukunai.meaning_mnemonic: Take something <radical>small</radical> — that hook with two flanking dots — and slice one more dot away with a downward stroke. Now there's even less than small: barely anything left. When you take a bite out of small, what remains is few.
n5-sukunai.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, opens his white-gloved hand to reveal only a few crumbs of confetti — "<reading>しょう</reading> time!" he squeaks, and even the doves look unimpressed by how little there is. His whole act, like everything about him, is small and few.
n5-sukunai.description: 少 is 小 with one extra stroke: a slash sweeping down and to the left below the base. Take that tail away and you are back to 小.

n5-suwaru.meaning_mnemonic: Two of those striding <radical>person</radical> figures come in from the cold and duck under the lean-to <radical>shelter</radical> nailed into the rock face, out of the rain at last. They drop straight down onto the same patch of <radical>earth</radical> underneath it, shoulder to shoulder, and flatly refuse to get up again. Two walkers on the ground under a roof want exactly one thing: to sit.
n5-suwaru.reading_mnemonic: The person who settles onto that patch of earth is Zara, and the moment she sits she lets out a long, satisfied "<reading>ざ</reading>あ" of relief. Every time you see someone plop down here, you hear Zara's ざ.
n5-suwaru.description: Means "sit"; shows up in words about sitting down, seats, and taking a seat.

n5-taberu.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the whole character as a little tent pitched over a full table: the peaked roof on top, and underneath it a heaped tray of rice and side dishes. It's the family shelter you duck into when you're hungry — a roof made entirely of dinner. Under that roof there's only one thing to do: eat the food.
n5-taberu.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful line cook at Koichi's konbini slings hot lunches under the fluorescent lights, and every time a tray lands he shouts his catchphrase: <reading>しょく</reading>, しょく, come and get it! You hear しょく and your stomach knows it's time to eat.
n5-taberu.description: Means eat or food; shows up in everyday words for meals, eating, and food, and as the verb "to eat."

n5-takai.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tall</radical> tower with windows standing over the town — but notice the open <radical>mouth</radical> at its base, an entrance yawning wide for anyone brave enough to climb. It's the fanciest, most expensive building around, and everyone cranes their neck to see how tall it is.
n5-takai.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, is jealous of that tall tower, so he stacks his onigiri shelves higher and higher until they're the tallest — and priciest — display in town. As the tower of rice balls wobbles, he shouts <reading>こう</reading> to warn a customer before it topples.

n5-tatsu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person planted firmly on the ground, feet apart, refusing to budge — they <radical>stand</radical> there, solid and upright. That single image, a person rooted on the earth, is the whole character: to stand.
n5-tatsu.reading_mnemonic: A soldier named Ritsu snaps to attention on the mountain trail, standing so straight you could measure a wall against him. Every time someone shouts "<reading>りつ</reading>!" he stands up even taller.
n5-tatsu.description: Means "stand"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words about standing up, standing something upright, and establishing or setting things in place.

n5-te-hand.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you can see the fingers spreading out from a wrist. That's the whole picture: fingers plus a wrist, held up for you to shake. It's a <radical>hand</radical>.
n5-te-hand.reading_mnemonic: A magician named Shu reaches out a bare hand and, with a flick, pulls a coin from behind your ear. As the coin lands in her palm she winks and says, "<reading>しゅ</reading>, that's all in the hand."
n5-te-hand.description: Means "hand"; a very common kanji that appears in everyday words for hands, gestures, and doing things by hand.

n5-ten.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a stick figure standing with arms flung wide, and someone has peeled up the flat horizon, the one long level <radical>ground</radical> you stand on, and laid it right across the top of those outstretched arms. The ground is up there now, a ceiling stretched over the whole world. Ground hanging above everyone's head is the ceiling of everything: heaven, the sky.
n5-ten.reading_mnemonic: A tent-pitcher hikes to the top of the mountain trail and, instead of camping on the ground, throws a giant tent (<reading>てん</reading>) up into the air to sleep among the clouds. When you crane your neck at the sky, you spot that tent (てん) floating right there in heaven.
n5-ten.description: 天 is 大 with an extra horizontal laid across the top, above the outstretched arms. 大 has one horizontal, 天 has two.

n5-tomeru.meaning_mnemonic: You're mid-stride down the mountain trail when you plant one foot flat and hard against the ground and freeze in place. That single planted foot is the whole picture: it's rooted, going nowhere. A planted foot means <radical>stop</radical>.
n5-tomeru.reading_mnemonic: Right where you stopped, you hear a sharp "<reading>し</reading>!" — someone shushing you. It's the vending machine at the top of the trail, hissing "し, し" as it refuses to dispense until you stop and wait. That shushing し is the sound to hold onto.
n5-tomeru.description: Means "stop" and is the base of common verbs like 止まる and 止める, showing up anywhere something halts or is brought to a halt.

n5-uenagashi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single flat line of <radical>ground</radical>, and standing on it a tortoise squinting at the cracks in its own shell. Its <radical>divination</radical> keeps coming out the same, so it plants one claw pointing straight at the sky and refuses to lower it. Everything in this shape leans away from the ground and skyward: up, above.
n5-uenagashi.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful mountaineer plants her flag at the summit and shouts "Joe!" as she looks up at the sky — <reading>じょう</reading> rings out across the peak. Every time you look up and above you, you hear her じょう echoing back down.
n5-uenagashi.description: Means "up" or "above"; a very common N5 kanji appearing in words for direction, position, and going up.

n5-uru-baku.meaning_mnemonic: The armoured <radical>samurai</radical> duck has abandoned the garden wall and set up a stall, balanced on a pair of sturdy <radical>human legs</radical> planted wide behind a table of stacked goods, an awning pulled taut over the lot as a <radical>cover</radical> against the rain. It still refuses to blink, it refuses to come down on the price, and it shouts at everyone who slows down. A samurai under his awning on braced legs has exactly one job: to sell.
n5-uru-baku.reading_mnemonic: The vendor keeps yelling one thing at every customer who walks past: "Buy! <reading>ばい</reading>, ばい, one for you and one for the baby!" He'll sell to anyone who slows down, and every pitch ends on that same ばい.

n5-ushiro.meaning_mnemonic: The penguin in the tipped hat commits to one enormous sideways <radical>step</radical> across the buttered kitchen floor, and snagged on its heel is a <radical>tiny thread</radical>, that flimsy dangling loop, with the duckling still tied to the far end. So the duckling gets towed along as a permanent <radical>trailing foot</radical>, one webbed foot skidding a full body-length back. Whatever the penguin does, the duckling comes after, behind.
n5-ushiro.reading_mnemonic: The trailing runner finally staggers across the finish line, dead last, and gasps out a weak "<reading>ご</reading>... ご..." — trying to say "go" but only managing to arrive after everyone else. That breathless ご is the sound that lands whenever this kanji shows up.

n5-yama.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape and count them: three peaks rising side by side, the middle one tallest. You don't need a story here — the character is a picture. Those three peaks are a <radical>mountain</radical>.
n5-yama.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine has a face, and it greets every exhausted hiker like an old friend: "You made it — welcome, san (<reading>さん</reading>)!" It calls everyone さん because on this mountain, reaching the peak earns you respect.
n5-yama.description: Means "mountain"; a common N5 kanji seen in nature words and countless place and family names.

n5-yasui.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>woman</radical> kneeling gracefully inside a snug little house, the <radical>roof</radical> pulled down over her like a blanket. Nothing can reach her in here — she is safe, the rent is nothing, everything is calm. A woman tucked safely under a roof is cheap and peaceful.
n5-yasui.reading_mnemonic: She's spreading sweet red <reading>あん</reading> (bean paste) on a bun, humming, utterly at peace. Every bite is cheap comfort — say あん and taste that calm.
n5-yasui.description: 安 means cheap or peaceful, and shows up in words for low prices, safety, and being at ease.

n5-yasumu.meaning_mnemonic: You're on the mountain trail and you spot a <radical>person</radical> (left) who has slumped sideways against a <radical>tree</radical>, leaning into the trunk with its roots and branches like it's the comfiest chair in the world. A <radical>person</radical> plus a tree they're propped against — that's someone taking a well-earned rest.
n5-yasumu.reading_mnemonic: The hiker leaning on that tree lets out a huge, happy sigh — "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" — the sound of every muscle finally letting go. Every time you picture that person melting into rest, you hear that きゅう escape.
n5-yasumu.description: Means "rest" and shows up in everyday words for taking breaks and days off, like 休み.

n5-yon.meaning_mnemonic: You peer into the closed box of the <radical>enclosure</radical>, walls all around, and inside you find a <radical>mouth</radical> trapped in the corner. It sits there counting on its lips, and the number it keeps landing on is four. An enclosure with a mouth inside: four.
n5-yon.reading_mnemonic: Inside those walls, a tiny shopkeeper named Shi is stacking exactly four onigiri and hissing "<reading>し</reading>, し, し" as she counts. Every time she runs out of breath, she's counted to four.
n5-yon.description: 四 and 西 are both boxes with strokes inside. 四 is a plain rectangle with two short strokes bending inward. 西 sits an extra horizontal bar above the box, which 四 never has.
